desc:
The alphabet is cyclic: after z comes a again. The distance between two letters is the shorter way around the cycle, so dist('a','c') = 2 and dist('a','z') = 1.

You may turn s into any string t of the same length as long as the total distance dist(s[0],t[0]) + dist(s[1],t[1]) + ... is at most k. Return the lexicographically smallest string t you can obtain.

s = "zbbz", k = 3  -> "aaaz"
s = "xaxcd", k = 4 -> "aawcd"
s = "lol", k = 0   -> "lol"
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Lexicographically smallest: the first letter is the most important. Can you turn it into a within the budget?
The cost of turning a letter into a is min(c, 26 - c) where c is its position in the alphabet counted from 0. Pay it whenever you can afford it, from left to right.
When the cost of reaching a exceeds what is left, spend all the remaining budget moving that letter backwards in the alphabet (chr(ord(c) - left)), then stop: everything to the right stays unchanged.
editorial: A smaller letter at an earlier position beats any gains later, so process the positions from left to right and make each one as small as the remaining budget allows.

For a letter with 0-based index c, reaching a costs d = min(c, 26 - c). If d ≤ left, set the letter to a and subtract d. Otherwise the budget cannot get this letter to a; the smallest reachable letter is obtained by moving it down by exactly left places (cost left), because here left < d ≤ 13 so going backwards costs exactly its step count. Then the budget is empty and the rest of the string is left unchanged.
Spending budget on an earlier letter is always at least as valuable as on a later one, which justifies the left-to-right order. One pass, O(n).
